figures.caption: Investigating the effect of different size marble chips on the rate of reaction between calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid

specPoints.text: practical: investigate the effect of changing the surface area of marble chips and of changing the concentration of hydrochloric acid on the rate of reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid
describe experiments to investigate the effects of changes in surface area of a solid, concentration of a solution, temperature and the use of a catalyst on the rate of a reaction

primer.text: From Measuring Rates you already know the gas-collection set-up that times a fizzing reaction. This practical aims that apparatus at marble chips, varying only their size to expose the surface area effect. The conclusion you draw at the end restates collision theory in chips and acid.

lessons.title: Marble chips and gas collection
lessons.opening: Calcium carbonate chips meet dilute hydrochloric acid in the classic rate practical. This lesson states the aim, lists the apparatus and walks the five-step method that fills the results table.
keyPoints: The aim is to investigate the effect of changing surface area on the rate of reaction.
A fixed volume of hydrochloric acid is placed in a conical flask connected to an inverted measuring cylinder.
Marble chips are added, the bung is closed, and the gas volume in a fixed time is recorded.
The method is repeated with different sizes of marble chips for comparison.
The investigation covers both chip size and acid concentration on the marble chip reaction.

low.restatement: Pour the same amount of acid into a flask, drop in chips of one size, and measure how much gas appears in a set time. Swap in bigger or smaller chips and run it again to compare. Only the chip size changes from one run to the next.
low.analogy: It is like timing how fast a sugar cube and the same sugar crushed dissolve; only the piece size changes.
low.examPointer: Name the fixed acid volume, the timed gas reading and the one factor varied between runs.

medium.restatement: A fixed volume of hydrochloric acid reacts with marble chips inside a sealed flask whose delivery tube feeds an inverted measuring cylinder, and the gas collected in a fixed time is recorded. The run is repeated with different chip sizes so that surface area is the only factor changing between experiments.
medium.analogy: Each run is a race between the acid and a fresh team of chips; the race clock and the track stay identical while only the team size differs.
medium.examPointer: Describe apparatus and timing first, then stress that chip size is the single varied factor.

check.stem: What does the inverted measuring cylinder collect in this practical?

options.text: The carbon dioxide gas released as the chips react with the acid
options.explanation: The fizzing between calcium carbonate and acid releases gas that is collected for measurement.

options.text: Leftover acid pushed out of the flask
options.explanation: Only gas travels down the delivery tube.

options.text: Dissolved marble chips
options.explanation: Solids stay in the flask.

options.text: Water from the trough
options.explanation: Water enters nothing; gas pushes water out of the cylinder.

check.stem: Why must the volume of acid stay fixed across all runs?

options.text: So that chip size is the only factor affecting the measured rate
options.explanation: A fair test changes one factor at a time and holds the rest constant.

options.text: Because acid is expensive
options.explanation: Cost is not the experimental reason.

options.text: Because the cylinder cannot hold more acid
options.explanation: Apparatus capacity is not the reason.

options.text: So the acid never runs out mid-run
options.explanation: Supply is not the design principle; fairness is.

check.stem: What timing rule applies to every run of the method?

options.text: Gas volume is recorded after the same fixed time in each run
options.explanation: A shared time window makes the volume readings comparable.

options.text: Each run lasts until all the chips dissolve
options.explanation: Runs to completion would take different times and defeat the comparison.

options.text: Each run is timed until the acid boils
options.explanation: Nothing boils in this practical.

options.text: Timing is unnecessary because gas volume alone suffices
options.explanation: Without a shared window, volumes mean different rates.

check.stem: The practical also investigates changing the concentration of the hydrochloric acid. Which factor does that vary?

options.text: The strength of the acid solution
options.explanation: Concentration is the acid-side factor paired with chip size in this investigation.

options.text: The temperature of the acid
options.explanation: Temperature is a different rate factor, not the one named here.

options.text: The size of the chips
options.explanation: That is the first factor; the second varies the acid.

options.text: The volume of gas collected
options.explanation: Gas volume is the measurement, not the varied factor.

check.stem: Which prediction follows from collision theory before the runs begin?

options.text: Smaller chips should give a faster reaction because more surface is exposed
options.explanation: More exposed particles means more collisions per second with the acid.

options.text: Smaller chips should react more slowly because they are lighter
options.explanation: Mass is unchanged by crushing; exposure rises.

options.text: Chip size cannot affect the rate
options.explanation: Surface area is a named rate factor.

options.text: Only the temperature could change the rate
options.explanation: Several factors including surface area act on rate.

lessons.title: Results and the collision conclusion
lessons.opening: The results table pairs each chip size with the gas volume collected in thirty seconds. This lesson reads the table, then states the collision-theory conclusion the data supports.
keyPoints: Results are recorded in a table of chip size against the volume of gas produced in thirty seconds.
Bigger exposed surfaces of the chips push the rate of reaction up.
More surface particles of the chips are exposed to the dilute hydrochloric acid.
The extra exposure produces more frequent and successful collisions.
The increased collision count raises the rate of reaction.

low.restatement: The table shows bigger gas volumes for the smaller chips, because crushed chips put more particles where the acid can reach. That is the surface area effect written in one line.
low.analogy: It is like handing out leaflets: a crowd of helpers on every corner reaches far more people than one helper standing still.
low.examPointer: Quote the trend from the table and finish with the exposed-particles explanation.

medium.restatement: The recorded gas volumes rise as the chip size falls, showing that a greater surface area increases the rate of reaction. More surface particles of the marble are exposed to the acid, so more frequent and successful collisions occur each second.
medium.analogy: A torn-open tea bag brews faster than a sealed one because twice the leaf meets the water; chips behave the same way in acid.
medium.examPointer: Link the measured trend to exposed surface particles and the collision language examiners expect.

check.stem: What belongs in the results table?

options.text: Chip size alongside the gas volume collected in thirty seconds
options.explanation: Those two columns carry everything needed to compare rates.

options.text: Time of day for each run
options.explanation: Clock time is irrelevant to the comparison.

options.text: The colour of the solution
options.explanation: Colour does not enter this measurement.

options.text: Chip mass only
options.explanation: The varied factor is size, recorded with the gas reading.

check.stem: What trend does the completed table show?

options.text: Smaller chips produce more gas in the same time, showing a faster rate
options.explanation: Greater surface area raises the collision count and the gas volume.

options.text: Larger chips produce more gas because they weigh more
options.explanation: Mass does not decide the rate; exposure does.

options.text: All sizes produce identical gas volumes
options.explanation: The whole point of the practical is the difference.

options.text: Gas volume falls as rate rises
options.explanation: Faster rate means more gas within the window.

check.stem: Which explanation supports the conclusion drawn from the results?

options.text: More exposed surface particles meet the acid, so more frequent and successful collisions occur
options.explanation: That is the collision-theory chain behind the surface area effect.

options.text: The acid becomes warmer around smaller chips
options.explanation: No temperature change is part of this design.

options.text: Small chips lower the activation energy
options.explanation: Only catalysts lower the barrier.

options.text: Small chips make the acid more concentrated
options.explanation: The acid concentration is fixed by the experimenter.

check.stem: A run with powder rather than chips gives a much larger gas reading. What does this confirm?

options.text: Powder exposes the greatest surface area, giving the fastest rate tested
options.explanation: Powder is the extreme end of the size trend.

options.text: Powder changes the products of the reaction
options.explanation: The chemistry is identical; only the pace differs.

options.text: Powder makes the reaction endothermic
options.explanation: Energy direction is unrelated to particle size.

options.text: Powder proves the acid was stronger
options.explanation: Acid strength is controlled and constant.

check.stem: Which sentence states the conclusion of the whole practical?

options.text: Increasing the surface area of the marble chip increases the rate of reaction
options.explanation: That single sentence captures the trend and its direction.

options.text: Increasing chip size increases the rate of reaction
options.explanation: The trend runs the other way.

options.text: Surface area has no measurable effect
options.explanation: The data shows a clear effect.

options.text: Rate depends only on the acid volume
options.explanation: Acid volume was held constant precisely so it would not decide the outcome.

glossary.definition: Lumps of calcium carbonate used as the solid reactant in this rate investigation.
The shared time window, such as thirty seconds, during which gas volume is recorded for every run.
The amount of solid surface exposed to the acid, increased by using smaller chips.
An experiment design in which only one factor changes while the rest are held constant.
The number of particle collisions per second, which rises with exposed surface area.

workedExample.prompt: Describe the experiment that investigates the effect of surface area on the rate of reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid, state the expected trend, and explain it using collision theory.
steps: Add a fixed volume of dilute hydrochloric acid to a conical flask connected by a delivery tube to an inverted measuring cylinder.
Add marble chips, close the bung, and record the volume of gas produced in a fixed time (30 seconds).
Repeat with different sizes of marble chips, keeping everything else the same, and record chip size against gas volume.

The smaller the chips, the greater the gas volume collected: increasing the surface area increases the rate, because more surface particles of the marble are exposed to the acid, giving more frequent and successful collisions.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Fixed-time gas volume per chip size; smaller chips react faster — more exposed surface particles give more frequent and successful collisions.
